Axum is the default choice for new Rust services: built on hyper and tower, maintained by the Tokio team, and free of macro DSLs.

Why Axum

  • Extractors instead of macros — a handler is a plain async fn whose arguments are typed requests.
  • tower middleware — the same layer works on any tower service, so timeouts, retries and load balancing compose.
  • No hidden magic — no #[get("/x")] attributes, no global router.
  • Types all the way down — a malformed path parameter is a 400 before your code runs.

Minimal server

Graceful shutdown drains in-flight requests before exiting — required for zero-downtime deploys.

Routing

Gotcha: Axum 0.8 changed path parameters from :id to {id}. A :id route now fails at startup with a clear error — if you are following a tutorial that uses :id, it is for 0.7.

Extractors

An extractor is anything implementing FromRequestParts (or FromRequest if it consumes the body). The handler signature declares what it needs.

Order matters: the body extractor (Json) must be last, because it consumes the request body.

Extractor summary

Extractor Source Fails with
Path<T> URL path params 400
Query<T> query string 400
Json<T> JSON body 400/415
State<S> router state —
HeaderMap headers —
TypedHeader<T> one header, typed 400
Extension<T> request-scoped value (auth) 500 if missing
Request raw request —
Bytes / String raw body —

Custom extractors: authentication

This is the Axum pattern that pays off most: authorisation becomes part of the type signature, and a handler that needs a user cannot be written without one.

Application state

State<T> requires T: Clone. AppState is cheap to clone because everything inside is Arc or a pool handle.

Gotcha: never put a Mutex<HashMap> in AppState for real data. Use the database. In-memory state is lost on restart and does not survive multiple replicas.

Errors as responses

Two rules that matter in production: log the real error server-side, and return a generic message for 5xx. Leaking a SQL error string to a client is an information disclosure.

Middleware with tower

Layers apply bottom-up: the last .layer() is the outermost, so it sees the request first.

Rate limiting

Pagination, filtering, sorting

Testing handlers without a network

oneshot exercises the whole router — routing, extractors, middleware, error mapping — with no socket and no port. This is the fastest reliable test you can write.

OpenAPI

Production checklist

  • Graceful shutdown wired to SIGTERM
  • Request body size limit (2 MB is a sane default)
  • Timeout layer (30 s)
  • CORS configured explicitly, not Any, for browser-facing APIs
  • TraceLayer so every request has a span with method, path, status, latency
  • /healthz and /readyz (module 03.06)
  • Errors mapped to a stable JSON shape; 5xx bodies contain no internals
  • per_page clamped; no unbounded list endpoints
  • Pool max_connections set from the DB's limit, not left at default
  • Rate limit on auth endpoints specifically

Exercises

  1. Add a PATCH /users/{id} handler that accepts a partial body (Option<T> fields) and only updates provided fields.
  2. Write a custom extractor Pagination that parses and clamps page and per_page in one place.
  3. Add a middleware that logs the request id from a header, or generates one.
  4. Implement IntoResponse for ApiError such that sqlx::Error::RowNotFound becomes 404 and every other DB error becomes 500.
  5. Add a /metrics endpoint (module 03.06) and confirm it is excluded from the timeout layer.
  6. Write oneshot tests for a 200, a 404 and a 422.
